blocks.text: A suffix array is an array containing the starting indices of every suffix of a string, arranged so that the suffixes they point to are in sorted lexicographic (alphabetical) order.

For a string of length n, there are exactly n suffixes (including the whole string itself, and the single last character). Instead of storing those suffixes as actual substrings, which would waste a huge amount of memory, a suffix array stores just their starting positions, ordered by what the suffix at that position looks like when sorted.

For example, for "banana", the suffix array tells you which starting position produces the alphabetically smallest suffix, then the next smallest, and so on, without ever materializing the full list of suffix strings in memory.

This document covers exactly one structure inside the Strings pattern group: the suffix array, how to build it efficiently, its companion the LCP array, and the class of problems both unlock together.

content.title: 1. Why Suffix Arrays Are So Powerful

blocks.text: Once the suffixes of a string are sorted, many string problems that look intimidating collapse into simple array operations.
That is the entire appeal of a suffix array: it turns hard string questions into operations you already know how to do fast on a sorted array.

items: Pattern matching: checking whether a pattern occurs in the string becomes a binary search over the sorted suffixes, since any suffix that starts with the pattern sits in one contiguous block.

Repeated substrings: because sorted suffixes that share a long prefix sit next to each other, comparing only neighboring suffixes (the LCP array) reveals every repeated substring without comparing all pairs.
Longest common substring: concatenating two strings with a separator and building one suffix array over the combination turns a two-string problem into a single-array scan.
Counting distinct substrings, lexicographically smallest rotation, and many suffix automaton style problems all become tractable once suffixes are sorted.

blocks.text: A suffix array is one of the most versatile string structures in competitive programming, it is the array you reach for whenever a problem talks about substrings, repeats, or comparisons across many positions of the same string.
The most direct way to build a suffix array is to actually generate all n suffixes as real substrings, then hand them to a standard comparison sort.
This works, and for tiny strings it is perfectly fine. The problem is the cost.

items: Building all n suffixes as separate substrings costs O(n^2) time and space, since suffix at index 0 alone has length n.

Sorting n items costs O(n log n) comparisons, but each individual comparison between two suffixes can itself cost up to O(n) in the worst case (long common prefixes force the comparator to walk far into both strings).

blocks.text: Multiplying those together gives an overall O(n^2 log n) construction. For a string of length 100,000, that is far too slow, competitive programming and production string search both need something closer to O(n log n).

content.title: 3. The Doubling Technique: Sorting by Rank, Not Raw Characters

blocks.text: The naive approach is slow because every comparison re-reads raw characters from scratch. The doubling technique fixes this by reusing the work done in earlier rounds instead of recomputing it.
The core intuition is simple: we already know how the first half of two suffixes sorts, we just need to break remaining ties using that information, instead of re-comparing characters one by one.
How it works, round by round

items: Round 0: rank every suffix by its first 1 character. Equal characters get equal ranks.
Round 1: rank every suffix by its first 2 characters, using the pair (rank of first char, rank of next char) computed in round 0. Comparing two suffixes now costs O(1) instead of O(2).
Round 2: rank every suffix by its first 4 characters, using the pair of ranks from round 1 (each of which already summarizes 2 characters). Comparing two suffixes still costs O(1).
Round k: rank every suffix by its first 2^k characters, using the pair of ranks from round k-1, each already summarizing 2^(k-1) characters.

blocks.text: The comparison length doubles every round: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on, so after roughly log2(n) rounds the comparison length covers the entire string and every suffix has a fully distinct rank.

Each round only needs a sort keyed on a pair of small integers (the previous round's ranks), never on raw characters again. That is what makes the doubling trick fast: information from the previous round is reused to make every future comparison O(1).

Concretely, suppose two suffixes tie after comparing their first 2 characters. Round 2 does not re-read those 2 characters from the string, it looks up the rank already computed in round 1 for the next 2 characters of each suffix, and compares only that single pair of integers, an O(1) lookup instead of another character by character scan.

blocks.caption: Each round doubles the compared prefix length by reusing ranks from the previous round instead of re-reading characters.

content.title: 4. Suffix Array Construction Using Doubling (C++ Implementation)

blocks.text: Putting the doubling idea into code: each round sorts the suffix indices by the pair (rank[i], rank[i + k]), then derives a fresh rank array from that sorted order before doubling k.
Every round runs a full sort over n indices using a comparator that only ever looks up two rank values, an O(1) comparison, and there are O(log n) rounds since k doubles each time.

With std::sort doing the sorting, each round costs O(n log n), giving O(n log^2 n) overall, this is the version most people write by hand and is what is usually meant by the O(n log n) doubling technique in interviews and contests. Replacing std::sort with a radix sort on the bounded rank pairs turns each round into O(n), bringing the true total down to O(n log n) the doubling structure stays exactly the same either way.
The early exit if (rnk[sa[n-1]] == n-1) break; stops as soon as all n ranks are distinct, which in practice happens well before log2(n) full rounds for most real strings.

content.title: 5. The LCP Array: Suffix Array's Essential Companion

blocks.text: A suffix array alone tells you the order of the suffixes, but not how similar neighboring suffixes are. That is exactly what the LCP array (Longest Common Prefix array) adds.

lcp[i] stores the length of the longest common prefix between the suffix at sorted position i and the suffix at sorted position i-1 (its immediate neighbor in the sorted order). By convention lcp[0] = 0, since position 0 has no left neighbor.
Because sorted suffixes that share a prefix sit next to each other, the LCP array only ever needs to compare adjacent pairs, never all O(n^2) pairs of suffixes, to find every repeated substring.
The longest repeated substring in the whole string is simply the maximum value in the LCP array. Whichever adjacent pair of sorted suffixes shares the longest prefix marks where that repeat occurs.

blocks.caption: lcp[i] is the length of the shared prefix between neighboring suffixes in sorted order.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785250263273-437003853.png
blocks.alt: Longest repeated substring is the maximum value in the LCP array

content.title: 6. Kasai's Algorithm: Building the LCP Array in O(n)

blocks.text: Computing every lcp[i] from scratch by comparing characters directly would cost O(n) per pair, or O(n^2) overall. Once the suffix array already exists, Kasai's algorithm computes the entire LCP array in O(n) total instead.

The key observation: if suffix i and its predecessor in sorted order share a prefix of length h, then after removing the first character of both (moving to suffix i + 1 and its own sorted predecessor), the shared prefix length can drop by at most 1. That means the running match length h never has to restart from zero, it only ever decreases by one step at a time between suffixes, so the total work across the whole pass stays linear.

Kasai's algorithm walks suffixes in their original string order (i = 0, 1, 2, ...), not sorted order, it uses the rankOf array to look up where each suffix sits inside the suffix array, then compares it only against its true neighbor in sorted order.
This is the standard companion to a suffix array in practice, build the suffix array first with doubling in O(n log n), then run Kasai's algorithm once to get the LCP array in O(n).

blocks.text: So LCP = [0, 1, 3, 0, 0, 2]. The maximum value is 3, occurring between "ana" (index 3) and "anana" (index 1), so the longest repeated substring in "banana" is "ana", which indeed occurs starting at both index 1 and index 3.
Pattern matching in O(m log n)

Every suffix that starts with a given pattern of length m sits in one contiguous block of the sorted suffix array, because sorted order groups suffixes with the same prefix together. That means checking whether the pattern occurs at all, or finding every occurrence, reduces to a binary search over the suffix array, comparing the pattern against a suffix costs O(m), and binary search costs O(log n) comparisons, for a total of O(m log n) per query.
Longest repeated substring

As shown in the worked example above, once the LCP array exists, the longest repeated substring is found in a single linear scan by taking the maximum value in the LCP array, no extra construction needed.
Longest common substring between two strings

Concatenate the two strings with a separator character that appears nowhere in either string, for example s1 + "#" + s2, and build one suffix array over the combined string. Then scan the LCP array looking for the maximum lcp[i] value where the two neighboring suffixes originate from different original strings (one starts before the separator, one starts after it). This turns a two-string problem into a single suffix array plus a linear scan.

items: Forgetting the sentinel or separator character when a suffix runs off the end of the string during comparison, treat a missing character as smaller than every real character (using -1 as in the implementation above), otherwise suffixes near the end compare incorrectly.

Off by one errors in the doubling comparator the second half of the comparison key is rank[i+k], not rank[i+k-1] or rank[i+k+1], a shifted index silently produces a wrong order that still looks plausible.
Confusing suffix array indices with LCP array positions lcp[i] is defined between SA[i] and SA[i-1], it is offset by one relative to the suffix array, not aligned to the same starting index.

Using the wrong string when concatenating for longest common substring without a unique separator that appears in neither string, a match can incorrectly span across the boundary between the two original strings.

Rebuilding the suffix array from scratch instead of using Kasai's algorithm for the LCP array wastes the O(n log n) work already done, Kasai's algorithm only needs O(n) more once the suffix array is known.
Hard Longest Duplicate Substring (LC 1044): binary search on answer length combined with suffix array style hashing, or a direct LCP array maximum.
Hard Longest Common Substring between two strings: concatenate with a separator and build a single suffix array plus LCP array.
Medium Count Distinct Substrings of a string: sum of n-SA[i]-lcp[i] across all sorted positions.
Medium Shortest Unique Substring or Repeated Substring Pattern style problems: driven directly by LCP array values.
Hard Suffix array based string matching for multiple pattern queries against the same text, where a Trie or repeated linear search would be too slow.
